title: One Word, and a Whole Sentence After It

blocks.title: You'll want to know first — что

segments.text: что — (tire) shto — (tire) what.
Read the spelling and then read the sound again, because they disagree. The word is written with ч, and it is said with a ш: shto, never chto.

That is not carelessness. It is one of a small handful of Russian words where the old spelling was kept after the pronunciation moved, and it is the commonest of them, so it is worth learning as a fact about this word rather than as a rule.
что (shto)? on its own is already a whole question, and it is the plainest way to ask somebody to say a word again. A single word, a rising voice, and one mark at the end.

blocks.title: The word, taken apart — the question family opens

segments.text: что (shto) goes back to PIE kʷid, "what" — (tire) the same word as Latin quid and English what itself.

You have met this family before. The farewell пока was built on the ancient question-stem kʷo-, the one behind как and the entire English wh- set. что (shto) is that family's plainest member, and the book collects the rest of it over the chapters that follow.

blocks.title: Grammar lens — the same word, doing the other job

segments.text: Put что (shto) between two clauses instead of at the front of a question, and it stops asking and starts carrying:
я знаю, что ты понимаешь — (tire) ya znáyu, shto ty panimáyesh — (tire) I know that you understand.
Three things to notice, and the third is the one to hold on to.
The comma is compulsory. Russian puts one in front of что (shto) every single time, with no exceptions of the kind English allows.
The English that can be dropped — (tire) I know you understand is perfectly good English. The Russian что (shto) cannot. Leave it out and the sentence breaks.
As a joining word it is said the way it is spelled: chto, not shto. Same letters, two jobs, two pronunciations.
English plays the same trick, twice: what and that both began as question words and one of them settled into this job.

segments.text: May the Russian что be dropped the way English drops that? (No — (tire) never.) What must always stand in front of it? (A comma.) Which of the two jobs is said shto? (The question.) And one look back: which eye-word did глаз push out of everyday Russian? (The word око, which survives inside очки, "little eyes.")

segments.text: думать has been in this book since the verbs of the mind, and until this chapter it had nothing to think about — (tire) no object bigger than a single word could be attached to it. что (shto) fixes that in one move:
я думаю, что … — (tire) ya dúmayu, shto … — (tire) I think that …

Whatever you can already say in Russian, you can now say you think it. That is a genuine step up rather than one more phrase: it turns every sentence you own into an opinion you have marked as your own, which is the difference between reporting a fact and taking a position.
я думаю, что ты понимаешь — (tire) ya dúmayu, shto ty panimáyesh — (tire) I think that you understand.
The comma before что (shto) is compulsory here as everywhere.

blocks.title: Grammar lens — the other frame, and the negative one

segments.text: знать takes что (shto) exactly as думать does, and the negative is where it earns its place:
я знаю, что (shto) ты понимаешь — (tire) I know that you understand.
я не знаю, что ты говоришь — (tire) ya ne znáyu, shto ty gavarísh — (tire) I do not know what you are saying.

Read those two English translations again. The Russian word is the same word both times, and English needs that in the first and what in the second. Russian makes no such split, which is one distinction fewer for you to get wrong.

The second sentence is the useful one. Until now this book could say я не знаю and stop — (tire) a flat shrug. With что (shto) you can say what it is you do not know, which is what turns an admission into something the other person can act on.

Which two verbs now take a whole sentence after them? (думать and знать.) And one look back: which farewell is built on the word for morning? (That is до завтра.)

blocks.title: Writing — one long stroke on the line

segments.text: Russian's dash is тире, and it is a genuinely long mark — (tire) longer than an English hyphen, with a space on each side of it:
брат — (tire) друг.
Draw it at the height of the small letters, not at the top and not on the baseline, and give it the length of about two letters.
The mark is a French loan, tiret, borrowed whole. What Russian does with it is not French at all.

blocks.title: Grammar lens — the mark for a verb that is not there

segments.text: You learned early that Russian says I am a student with no verb in the middle: the present tense of быть is absent altogether. On the page, that absence gets a mark of its own.
Where the sentence would have needed is, and both halves are nouns, a Russian writer puts a dash:
сестра — (tire) подруга.

A sister is a friend. There is no verb in that sentence and there never will be. The dash is doing its work — (tire) and it is the only punctuation mark in the language whose job is to stand in for a word.
Say it aloud and there is a small pause exactly where the dash sits. The mark is not decoration; it is written-down silence.
